productBrief: Reviewers value Instagram for staying in touch with friends and family, and that is the clearest positive signal here. The largest problem by volume is accounts -- some held for over a decade -- suspended with no specific reason and no reachable human to appeal to, with a related group locked out by recovery flows that assume a device or number they no longer have. A third group describes the feed, including the 'Following' filter, crowded out by ads and suggested posts.

strengths.whatUsersValue: A recurring group of reviewers describe Instagram in simple relational terms -- a way to stay in touch with friends and family and feel connected -- rather than describing any single feature.
strengths.whyThisMatters: This is the app's most basic value proposition and, in a sample otherwise dominated by account-access and moderation complaints, it's notable that the core social function itself is still what satisfied reviewers point to.
strengths.protectThis: Whatever currently makes the app feel personally connective (seeing friends' posts, messaging) should be protected as feed-algorithm and moderation changes are made in response to the pain points below -- several pain points below directly describe this connective experience being crowded out by ads and suggested content.

strengths.whatUsersValue: A smaller group of reviewers specifically credit Instagram with helping them grow a personal brand, creative practice, or small business, distinct from the general social-connection praise above.
strengths.whyThisMatters: Two reviewers credit Instagram with helping them build a business or brand. Two others in the same sample say the opposite -- that their reach is suppressed unless they pay. Both are shown, because a growth claim resting on two positive accounts should be read next to the reviewers reporting the reverse.
strengths.protectThis: Discoverability and reach for creators/businesses is what this group values; the feed-algorithm complaints elsewhere in this sample (accounts not reaching people who already follow them) are a direct risk to this specific value driver.

painPoints.theme: Account Bans & Suspensions Without Clear Cause or Appeal
painPoints.affectedJourney: Using an existing account, or creating a new one, without triggering an automated suspension or permanent ban.

userImpact.reasoning: Reviewers describe losing access to accounts held for years -- along with photos, messages, and social connections -- with no explanation of the specific violation and no way to reach a person to appeal, which fully blocks continued use of the app for those affected rather than degrading it.

strategicRelevance.reasoning: An account is the precondition for every other feature; losing access to it without recourse is as core a failure as a navigation app routing you nowhere.

evidenceConfidence.reasoning: Thirteen reviewers independently describe the same pattern -- an account suspended or banned with no stated reason, no access to a human reviewer, and repeated failure of new accounts to survive -- with enough consistency (many explicitly say 'no reason given') that this reads as a systemic pattern rather than isolated moderation misses.

painPoints.synthesis: A large and consistent group of reviewers describe accounts -- some held for many years -- being suspended or permanently banned with no specific reason given, no accessible human reviewer, and in several cases new replacement accounts being suspended again shortly after creation. Several reviewers explicitly attribute this to increased automated (AI) moderation without human oversight, though that attribution is the reviewers' own theory, not something this analysis can independently verify.
painPoints.potentialImplication: Because this affects the precondition for using the app at all, and several reviewers describe it recurring across repeated account-creation attempts, unresolved instances could plausibly drive affected users to competing platforms entirely, not just reduce engagement.
painPoints.recommendedNextStep: Audit a sample of suspended/banned accounts against the specific policy violation cited (if any), and validate whether an accessible human-appeal path currently exists and how long it takes to reach a resolution.
painPoints.likelyImplementationSurface: Automated content/account moderation systems and the appeal/support routing flow.
painPoints.implementationConsiderations: Whether enforcement is genuinely over-triggering versus users under-recalling a real violation can't be determined from review text alone; the more verifiable and actionable part of this pattern is the reported absence of a reachable human appeal path.

painPoints.affectedJourney: Recovering access to an existing, non-banned account after a lost device, forgotten password, or routine security prompt.

userImpact.reasoning: Distinct from the moderation pain point above, this is about legitimate account owners -- not accused of any violation -- being unable to complete the recovery flow at all, permanently losing access to accounts held for years.

strategicRelevance.reasoning: A broken recovery flow fails the same precondition (account access) as a wrongful ban, just via a different mechanism -- a technical/flow defect rather than a moderation decision.

evidenceConfidence.reasoning: Six reviewers describe related but not identical recovery failures (video-selfie verification looping, SMS codes never arriving, being required to use an authenticator app with no alternative, old-device dependency), which is a coherent theme but with somewhat varied specific failure points.

painPoints.synthesis: Reviewers describe being unable to regain access to legitimate, long-held accounts because the recovery flow requires something they no longer have -- access to an old device, a working SMS code, or an authenticator app -- with no alternative path offered and, in several cases, an AI chat assistant unable to help with account-specific problems.
painPoints.potentialImplication: Because these reviewers explicitly distinguish themselves from rule-breakers ('I've done nothing wrong'), a broken recovery flow could plausibly be read as a trust failure distinct from moderation policy -- a purely technical gap rather than an enforcement judgment call.
painPoints.recommendedNextStep: Validate whether the recovery flow has a fallback path for users who can no longer access their original device, phone number, or authenticator app, and confirm whether AI-assisted support can currently escalate unresolved cases to a human.
painPoints.likelyImplementationSurface: Account recovery and two-factor authentication flow.
painPoints.implementationConsiderations: Recovery flows must balance security against accessibility; without internal visibility into fraud rates, it's not possible to say from reviews alone whether the current flow is miscalibrated or appropriately strict.

painPoints.theme: Feed Prioritizes Ads & Suggested Content Over Followed Accounts
painPoints.affectedJourney: Opening the app to see updates from accounts the user actually follows.

userImpact.reasoning: Doesn't block use of the app, but reviewers describe the core browsing experience becoming actively unpleasant -- ads and suggested content crowding out the people they intentionally follow, including within the 'Following' filter meant to avoid exactly that.

strategicRelevance.reasoning: The feed is the primary surface for the app's core browsing/connection experience; its composition directly shapes daily use.

evidenceConfidence.reasoning: Six reviewers independently describe the same specific pattern -- ads and suggested/unfollowed content interleaved with or replacing followed-account posts, including in the supposedly-filtered 'Following' view -- with concrete before/after comparisons.

painPoints.synthesis: Reviewers describe the feed -- including the 'Following' filter specifically meant to show only followed accounts -- interleaved with ads and algorithmically suggested posts to the point that people they actually follow become hard to find. Several describe this as a change from how the feed used to behave; that comparison is their recollection, not a measured shift.
painPoints.potentialImplication: Because several reviewers frame this as the reason they're reducing use or considering leaving, sustained ad/suggestion density could plausibly suppress time spent with the app's core social-connection value, though this sample can't measure actual usage change.
painPoints.recommendedNextStep: Validate the actual ad/suggested-content ratio currently shown in the 'Following' feed view specifically against its intended design, since reviewers report ads appearing there despite the filter's purpose.
painPoints.likelyImplementationSurface: Feed ranking algorithm and the 'Following'-filtered feed view specifically.
painPoints.implementationConsiderations: Whether this reflects a recent ranking change or a 'Following' filter that never fully excluded ads is not determinable from review text alone.

painPoints.affectedJourney: General day-to-day use -- posting stories, editing a bio, receiving notifications, viewing saved content.

userImpact.reasoning: Individually disruptive but narrow in scope (a stuck translation setting, missing notifications, a broken cancel button) -- annoying rather than blocking for most reviewers.

strategicRelevance.reasoning: These are real defects but scattered across secondary features rather than the core feed, posting, or messaging experience.

evidenceConfidence.reasoning: Seven reviewers describe genuinely different bugs (translation stuck on one language, missing story highlights, freezing, notifications not firing), which is real but heterogeneous -- likely several small independent defects rather than one root cause.

painPoints.synthesis: A scattered set of specific defects recur with no common cause: a 'cancel upload' button that does nothing, a bio character limit rejecting input below its stated maximum, the app freezing shortly after opening, translation locked to one language, story highlights missing on mobile but present on web, a repost function never arriving, and notifications silently not firing despite correct settings. Grouped as a monitoring signal, not one defect.
painPoints.potentialImplication: Accumulated small defects across secondary features could plausibly erode confidence in overall app quality even without one severe failure.
painPoints.recommendedNextStep: Log and cluster these by app version and platform (iOS-specific effects are mentioned in some reports) to determine which are still live versus already fixed in a more recent release.
painPoints.likelyImplementationSurface: Several independent client-side features (notifications, localization, story highlights, media caching).
painPoints.implementationConsiderations: Heterogeneous symptoms make a single fix unlikely.

priorities.recommendedNextStep: Validate the actual ad/suggested-content ratio in the 'Following' feed view against its intended design.
priorities.likelyImplementationSurface: Feed ranking algorithm and the 'Following'-filtered feed view.

priorities.whyNow: Distinct from moderation bans, this affects legitimate account owners with no violation, and is a narrower technical/flow fix rather than a policy judgment call.

priorities.likelyImplementationSurface: Account recovery and two-factor authentication flow.
priorities.implementationConsiderations: Recovery flows must balance security against accessibility; internal fraud-rate data would be needed to calibrate any change.

14467887920.title: You Can Feel Yourself Rotting
14467887920.body:
It’s hard to imagine the Instagram of 10+ years ago compared to the Instagram of today. 

10 years ago you could scroll through your feed and see posts from your friends only, in chronological order, and once you were caught up there was no more feed. No endless scroll to suck you in and consume your thoughts and precious time. 

Today, Instagram has become an all seeing all consuming entity, determined to harvest your data and your energy at every possibly opportunity. 

Open your feed. First post from a friend. Next post is an ad. Next post is an ad. Next post is someone you don’t know, but it’s recommended for you. Next post is an ad. Next post if your friend, sharing a video from a few days ago. You click the video to make it full screen. You finish the video and give it a like, then mindlessly scroll down. Now it’s an hour later, you find yourself scrolling through reels endlessly. You aren’t even sure why you ended up in reels in the first place, or why you’ve wasted such time scrolling and scrolling. All the while you are being advertised to. Aggressively. Somehow Instagram knows that you did a google search for hair growth tips yesterday, now you’re seeing ads for hair transplants, hair growth medicines. 

There is almost a hypnotic effect at play here. Many times I have *snapped* out of the endless scroll and thought to myself “what am I doing? why am I doing this?”. It feels very gross. It has been designed to consume you while you consume it.  

What inspired me to leave this review was the ads. Over the last few days my ads have suddenly shifted. I have been BOMBARDED with military propaganda. Every single ad has been for either a branch of the military, or an org supporting the military, or a local credit union for the military, or it’s a wife showing you how great it is to be a military spouse. It’s all so sick, especially for someone with ANY awareness of what is going on in this country and in the world right now. 

I’m so sick of it all. This is a sick app, designed by sick people. It is meant to harvest every detail about your life while simultaneously enslaving you to…. anything. To scrolling. To envy. To propaganda.
